title: T and Y
summary: Two more index-finger reaches, and the letter that starts the most common word in English.
intro: T is the second most common letter in the language and Y closes the top row for your index fingers, so between them these two keys turn up in almost every sentence you will ever type. The reach is upward and inward — further than R and U, and easy to undershoot. Aim with the finger, not the wrist, and let the hand stay where it is.
congrats: With T you can type the, that, this and to — four of the ten most common words in English, all from one new key. Seventeen keys down, and the sentences are getting longer.

screens.text: Left index finger, up and one key inward from F. It is a longer stretch than R, so the temptation is to move the whole hand — resist it and let the finger do the reaching.
T, R, F, G — four keys, one finger, four directions. Come back to the bump between each one.
screens.content:
jrt gfd jr
gt tg gtgt
fff ggg tttt rrrr

screens.text: Right index finger, up and one key inward from J. The mirror of T, and the last of the six keys your index fingers are responsible for on the top row.
Y, U, J, H. Y is the furthest reach on this hand — if it starts to feel cramped, drop your wrist rather than twisting it.
screens.content:
ufd jkh uf
hj jh hjhj
hhh uuuu yyyy jjjj

screens.text: The four upper index-finger keys, alternating hands. Slow is fine; landing on the right key is the whole exercise.
Words built around T. Notice how often it arrives with H right after it — that pair is worth learning as one movement.
screens.content:
stay talk at let
till tried treats set
steal east this trades

screens.text: Now Y, which mostly turns up at the end of a word. Your little finger should still be resting on its home key while the index reaches.
screens.content:
sadly yard daily ugly
fairly hardly yeast stays
study likely yes dry

screens.text: A burst of short words carrying both new keys. Read the whole word before you start typing it.
Back to patterns for one screen, to check that the reaches still end at home. Both index fingers on their bumps between every stretch.
screens.content:
ty yt tyty
tttt yyyy fff jjjj
tytyty ytytyt

screens.text: Everything you have so far, five words to a line. Seventeen keys is enough for a surprising amount of ordinary English.
screens.content:
fridge large title refill deed
aid leak hardly rush highs
regard slide till judges trades

screens.text: Sentences again, longer than the ones in Unit 1. Still no capitals or full stops — those arrive at the end of this unit.
screens.content:
